key_insight: Two current-generation large language models performed at nearly identical, near-top levels on an anesthesiology in-training exam question bank, including figure-based items when images were provided.
clinical_relevance: These results suggest LLMs may be useful study aids in anesthesiology education, but they are not substitutes for clinician judgment or exam preparation tools that rely on verified content.
method: 1,001 single-best-answer anesthesiology ITE review questions were given to Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6.
Each question was asked once in a fresh, stateless context with no tools, retrieval, answer key, or explanation.
All 27 figure-dependent items were included; published figures were supplied for the image-based subset.
evidence_signal: Claude Opus 5 scored 947/1,001 (94.6%) and GPT-5.6 scored 946/1,001 (94.5%); the difference was not significant, and accuracy dropped sharply when figures were withheld from figure-based questions.
watch_item: Performance was measured on a review question bank rather than a live clinical setting, so educational usefulness may not translate directly to real-world decision support.
paper_title: Assessing the Performance of Artificial Intelligence on Anesthesiology In-Training Examinations and Applicability in Medical Education
